strengths: The paper proposes a simple and interesting formulation for radar-guided metric depth: predict scene-conditioned polynomial coefficients that transform frozen MDE outputs, rather than directly regressing dense depth or applying only scale-and-shift. This is a clean idea with low apparent overhead and a plausible motivation.

The empirical results are strong across three radar-camera datasets. PolyRad improves over recent baselines on nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft at 50/70/80m, with especially large gains on ZJU and VoD, and the main tables consistently support the claim that higher-order fitting outperforms linear fitting.

The ablations are useful: removing cross-modal attention, learnable radar prototypes, or the derivative regularizer degrades performance, and the polynomial-degree sweep shows a meaningful trend from degree 1 through degree 8 with slight overfitting at degree 10.

The method is tested with several MDE backbones on nuScenes, including DPT, Depth Anything, Depth Pro, and UniDepth, which supports the claim that the fitting mechanism is not tied to a single monocular depth model.
The manuscript is generally clear and well structured. The formulation, loss, and qualitative examples make the intended mechanism easy to understand.
weaknesses: A core limitation is that the final prediction is a scene-global polynomial function of the initial MDE depth value. Thus two pixels with the same MDE depth must receive the same metric depth, regardless of image location or local radar evidence. This restricts the method’s ability to fix spatially localized errors and weakens some claims about correcting object-level misalignments via learned correspondences.

The monotonicity regularizer is described as enforcing monotonicity, but penalizing |1 - d d_hat / dz| does not actually guarantee a positive derivative everywhere. It also targets slope 1 in the MDE-depth coordinate system, which may be poorly justified when the input is arbitrary scaleless depth or inverse depth. The paper should be more precise about this technical claim.

The evaluation lacks several details needed for reproducibility in the main paper: dataset split definitions, radar preprocessing, input resolution, training schedule, loss weights, number of prototypes, architecture dimensions, and whether all baselines were retrained under identical settings. Many details are deferred to supplementary material, which makes the main submission hard to independently assess.

Fairness of comparisons is not fully established. PolyRad uses a strong frozen MDE backbone, apparently UniDepth for the main results, but the main baseline table does not clearly state whether competing radar-camera methods receive comparable MDE priors or whether they are reproduced with matched backbones across all datasets.

The paper would benefit from stronger diagnostic experiments: performance versus radar point count/noise, weather/night subsets, scenes where MDE has local failures, cross-dataset generalization, runtime/parameter comparisons, and statistical variance over runs. These are important for a method motivated by robust radar-camera deployment.

Some originality claims are overstated. Polynomial or monotone calibration of model outputs is a classical idea; the novelty is its application to radar-conditioned depth fitting, not polynomial fitting for foundation-model adaptation in general. The paper should temper these broader claims.

strengths: The problem is relevant: turning monocular depth outputs into metric depth using cheap radar is important for autonomous-driving perception, and the paper targets a practical sensor configuration.

The method is simple and potentially useful if validated: predicting a small set of polynomial coefficients from radar/MDE features is computationally lighter than dense per-pixel refinement and could be an attractive calibration-style module.

The paper reports results on three radar-camera datasets, nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft, and includes comparisons at multiple maximum depth ranges. The reported improvements in Table 1 are large, especially on ZJU and View-of-Delft.

The paper includes some relevant ablations: polynomial degree, MDE backbone choice, learnable prototypes, cross-modality attention, and monotonicity loss. These suggest that the proposed components are not entirely incidental.
weaknesses: The central technical premise is not fully convincing. A single global polynomial f(z) applied to the MDE depth value cannot correct spatially dependent errors when different objects or regions have the same or similar MDE depth but require different metric depths. The radar features only predict scene-level coefficients after global aggregation, so the method cannot provide location-specific corrections despite repeatedly claiming object/local-region correction.

The monotonicity claim is overstated. Penalizing |1 - d d_hat/dz| at sampled pixels encourages slopes near 1 but does not guarantee monotonicity over the input depth range, does not prevent all oscillations between sampled values, and is not equivalent to a constrained isotonic regression formulation. This matters because the paper’s explanation relies heavily on preserving ordinal depth while allowing flexible corrections.

There is a conceptual tension between using inflection/non-monotonic flexibility to fix cross-object misalignment and imposing a derivative-near-one regularizer. If the MDE model truly orders objects incorrectly, a monotone global polynomial cannot reorder them; if the polynomial becomes non-monotone, local ordinal consistency is no longer protected. The paper does not resolve this contradiction.

The experimental comparison appears potentially unfair or under-controlled. PolyRad benefits from a strong modern MDE backbone, especially UniDepth, but Table 1 compares against radar-camera methods that may not use the same backbone or foundation-model prior. Table 2 compares RadarCam-Depth with several backbones, but the main SOTA claim still lacks a controlled comparison where competing fusion methods are upgraded comparably.

The ablations do not isolate the claimed contribution cleanly enough. Degree-1 polynomial is presented, but stronger scale/shift or monotone nonlinear calibration baselines, per-scene least-squares fits to radar points, splines/isotonic regression, MLP depth-value mappings, and spatially varying coefficient variants are missing. These would be natural baselines for the proposed polynomial-fitting idea.

Important reproducibility details are absent from the main manuscript: dataset splits, preprocessing, radar projection/filtering, input resolution, architecture dimensions, number of prototypes, polynomial normalization, loss weights, optimizer, training schedule, batch size, and model selection procedure. The paper repeatedly refers to supplementary material, but the provided manuscript alone is insufficient for reproduction.

The reported gains are large, but evidence breadth is thinner than the claims. There are no uncertainty estimates, no cross-dataset generalization tests, no robustness analysis under radar sparsity/noise/weather, and no failure cases. Given the method’s dependence on radar point quality and a tuned polynomial degree, these omissions are material.

The mathematical exposition contains questionable statements. For example, the paper loosely equates polynomial degree with inflection-point capacity and claims higher-order terms perform local depth adjustments, but the polynomial is global in the scalar depth value, not local in image space. These are more than presentation issues because they affect what the method can actually model.

The paper claims efficiency and simplicity but does not provide runtime, parameter count, memory, or training-cost comparisons in the main manuscript. This weakens one of the stated motivations relative to more complex fusion methods.

Clarity is adequate at a high level, but several claims are rhetorically stronger than the supporting evidence, including statements about being a foundation-model adaptation method for any task and about correcting cross-object misalignments. The paper would be stronger if these claims were narrowed to what the experiments actually demonstrate.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful idea: predicting scene-level polynomial coefficients from radar/MDE features to convert monocular depth outputs into metric depth. This is a simple, interpretable alternative to heavier radar-camera depth-completion pipelines.

The experimental results are strong across three datasets. On the reported 80m setting, PolyRad improves over the strongest baselines on nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft, with especially large gains on ZJU and VoD.

The ablations support the main design choices: reducing the polynomial to degree 1, removing cross-modal attention, removing learnable radar prototypes, or removing the derivative regularizer all degrades performance.
The method is modular with respect to the MDE backbone. The paper evaluates DPT, Depth Anything, Depth Pro, and UniDepth, and shows consistent gains over raw MDE and RadarCam-Depth variants.

The motivation is technically plausible and well communicated: a global scale-and-shift cannot correct non-uniform depth-range errors, while a constrained polynomial transformation can model depth-dependent corrections at low computational cost.
weaknesses: The claimed monotonicity constraint is somewhat overstated. Penalizing the derivative toward 1 encourages smooth local behavior, but it does not strictly guarantee a positive derivative everywhere, especially for high-degree polynomials and unnormalized depth ranges.

The transformation is global and depth-only once coefficients are predicted. Pixels with similar MDE depth receive similar polynomial correction, so the method may struggle with spatially varying errors or objects at similar predicted depths that require different metric corrections. The paper does not analyze this failure mode in depth.

Several implementation details appear deferred to the supplement or are insufficiently specified in the main paper, including exact architecture sizes, polynomial input normalization, loss weights, training schedule, radar preprocessing, and dataset split/protocol details. This weakens reproducibility from the manuscript alone.

The empirical evaluation is convincing on standard MAE/RMSE, but limited in diagnostic breadth. There is little analysis of robustness to radar sparsity/noise, adverse weather, calibration error, varying radar point counts, or out-of-distribution transfer, despite these being central motivations for radar use.

Some novelty claims are broader than the evidence supports, such as positioning polynomial fitting as a general strategy for adapting foundation model predictions beyond this task. The experiments only substantiate radar-guided depth estimation.

The comparisons would be stronger with clearer fairness details: whether all baselines were retrained under identical data, backbones, image resolutions, and evaluation masks, and whether runtime/parameter counts are measured rather than referenced as supplementary material.

strengths: The paper proposes a simple and interesting formulation: use radar-conditioned global polynomial coefficients to transform pretrained monocular depth predictions into metric depth. The shift from affine scale/shift calibration to nonlinear scene-level fitting is well motivated and technically plausible.

The empirical results are strong across three radar-camera datasets. POLAR improves over recent baselines on nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft, with especially large gains on ZJU and VoD, and also reports favorable latency and FLOPs.

The ablation suite is useful. The paper studies polynomial degree, MDE backbone choice, learnable prototypes, cross-modal attention, monotonicity regularization, radar point density, zero-shot transfer, and several regression/adaptation baselines.

The method is computationally attractive. Predicting a small number of coefficients and applying a polynomial transform is much lighter than dense decoding or multi-stage radar-camera completion pipelines.
The manuscript is generally clear, with a coherent method description and helpful qualitative comparisons.
weaknesses: Some technical claims are overstated. A single global polynomial maps identical or similar MDE depth values to identical or similar metric values regardless of image location, so it cannot truly make arbitrary spatially distinct local corrections or sharpen boundaries except through differences already present in the MDE depth. The paper sometimes attributes local structural improvements to the polynomial in a way that exceeds what the model class can express.

The monotonicity regularizer is not simply enforcing monotonicity; it penalizes the derivative toward 1. This is a stronger and somewhat under-justified constraint, especially when MDE outputs may be scaleless, inverse-depth, metric-depth, or differently normalized across backbones. The paper does not clearly explain normalization or numerical stability for high-degree powers such as degree 8.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important architecture details such as feature dimensions, prototype count, MLP/CNN structure, temperature choice, preprocessing, normalization, and precise baseline reproduction settings are not fully specified.

Some comparisons need more scrutiny. The baselines may use different MDE backbones or training setups, and the paper does not fully clarify whether all methods are retrained under identical data, augmentation, resolution, and evaluation protocols. This matters because the reported gains are partly tied to the strength of the frozen MDE backbone.

There are presentation and consistency issues in the appendix. For example, Table 6 labels the second dataset as VoD but reports values that appear to match ZJU in at least some rows, which undermines confidence in the ablation reporting.

The theoretical proof mainly shows that three points need not lie on a line, which is mathematically true but too weak to justify the stronger practical claim that high-degree global polynomial fitting is the right correction model for monocular depth errors.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: metric depth estimation from camera plus sparse automotive radar, where radar is cheaper and more robust than lidar but difficult to exploit due to sparsity and noise.

The proposed idea of learning a low-dimensional scene-level calibration of a frozen monocular depth estimator is appealing for efficiency. The reported runtime and FLOP numbers are strong, with POLAR faster than the listed radar-camera baselines.

The empirical section covers three relevant datasets, multiple distance thresholds, several MDE backbones, ablations over polynomial degree and architecture components, reduced-radar-density tests, and a zero-shot cross-dataset experiment. This is a broader evaluation than many papers in this area.
The ablations support that higher-order fitting, cross-modal fusion, and the monotonicity regularizer each contribute to the reported performance, at least under the authors' implementation.
weaknesses: The central technical claim is overstated. A global polynomial f(z) applied to the MDE depth value cannot correct spatially distinct regions that have the same or similar predicted z but require different metric depths; it can only remap depth values. This undermines claims about correcting object-level misalignments, sharpening boundaries, and preserving/extrapolating structure. The paper repeatedly attributes spatial/geometric correction ability to a scalar depth transform without sufficiently acknowledging this limitation.

The theoretical motivation is weak. The proof that three points may not be fit by a line is trivial and does not establish that a polynomial in monocular depth is the right model for radar-camera metric estimation. The Taylor approximation corollary assumes a smooth single-valued relationship d=f(z), which is exactly the questionable assumption in complex scenes.

The monotonicity regularizer is not fully convincing. Penalizing |1 - d d_hat/dz| encourages derivative near one, not merely positive monotonicity, and the behavior depends strongly on the scaling/normalization of z. The paper does not give enough detail on z normalization, clipping, numerical stability for z^8 or z^10, or how negative/invalid depths are prevented.

The comparison may be confounded by the use of a strong frozen MDE backbone, especially UniDepth. It is not clear that all baselines receive comparable monocular priors or are tuned/retrained under equally favorable conditions. Since the improvement over TacoDepth on nuScenes is modest, the claimed large average gains rely heavily on datasets/baselines where the fairness of backbone capacity matters.

Several evaluation details needed for reproducibility and interpretation are missing or under-specified: exact train/validation/test splits, lidar projection masks, cropping and resizing, radar preprocessing, MDE input resolution, coefficient-network architecture dimensions, number of prototypes, optimizer/batch size, data augmentation, and whether baseline numbers are reproduced or copied from papers under identical protocols.

The reported qualitative claims are stronger than what the method can structurally support. Since the output is a pointwise polynomial transform of the MDE map, geometric artifacts and missing structures can only be fixed if they already exist in the MDE prediction in a recoverable scalar-depth form. The manuscript should separate what comes from the MDE backbone from what the polynomial calibration actually changes.

The polynomial-degree study shows dataset-dependent tuning, but the paper presents degree 8 as generally effective without a principled selection method. This weakens deployment claims, especially for new domains or radar configurations.

Some SOTA and percentage-improvement claims are inflated or imprecise. On nuScenes, POLAR only slightly improves over TacoDepth, while TacoDepth is missing on View-of-Delft. The abstract’s large average improvement numbers obscure this uneven picture.

The paper is generally readable, but it contains presentation issues that affect technical clarity, including inconsistent claims about inflection points, degree of freedom arguments comparing pixels to radar points, and statements that higher-order terms provide high-frequency corrections even though the transform is global in z rather than spatially adaptive.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and useful idea: rather than directly decoding dense depth or applying only a global affine correction to monocular depth, it learns radar-conditioned polynomial coefficients to map MDE predictions into metric depth. This is a simple, well-motivated formulation with practical appeal.

The empirical results are strong across three radar-camera datasets. POLAR improves over recent baselines on nuScenes, ZJU-4DRadarCam, and View-of-Delft, with especially large gains on ZJU and VoD, while also reporting lower inference time and GFLOPs than prior methods.

The evaluation includes several valuable analyses beyond the main table: polynomial degree sensitivity, component ablations, multiple MDE backbones, reduced radar density, zero-shot transfer, and comparisons to regression-style alternatives such as isotonic regression, PCHIP, and adapter tuning.

The method is computationally attractive. Predicting a small number of global polynomial coefficients is much lighter than dense fusion/decoding approaches, and the reported 24.81 ms inference time on nuScenes supports the paper's deployment motivation.

The paper is generally well written and the core intuition is easy to follow. The figures, ablations, and appendix help explain why affine scale-and-shift corrections can be insufficient and why radar-conditioned nonlinear fitting may help.
weaknesses: The technical framing sometimes overstates what a global polynomial transform can do. Since the same scalar function f(z) is applied to every pixel, the method cannot distinguish two spatial regions with the same or similar MDE depth that require different metric corrections. This limits the claim that it can generally correct cross-object misalignment or sharpen fine boundaries; it can only do so to the extent those errors are separable in the MDE depth-value domain.

The monotonicity regularizer is presented as enforcing monotonicity, but the actual loss penalizes the derivative toward 1 rather than directly enforcing non-negativity. This may be a useful stabilizer, but the paper does not fully justify why unit slope is the right target given arbitrary MDE output scale, backbone-dependent depth normalization, and high-degree polynomial behavior.

Some important implementation details are under-specified for reproducibility, including exact architecture dimensions, number of prototypes, input normalization for MDE depths before exponentiation, coefficient constraints or numerical stabilization for high-degree terms, data preprocessing, and whether all baselines were retrained under identical conditions.

Baseline fairness is not completely transparent. POLAR appears to benefit from strong pretrained MDE backbones such as UniDepth, while it is not always clear whether competing methods use equally strong backbones or were adapted with the same input resolution, training budget, and data protocol. TacoDepth is also missing on View-of-Delft, weakening the completeness of that comparison.

The theoretical argument against affine scale-and-shift is mathematically true but fairly weak as a contribution: any three non-collinear pairs cannot be fit by a line. The more important empirical question is whether a single global polynomial is the right inductive bias for real scenes, and the paper only partially probes its failure modes.

The evaluation focuses mainly on MAE/RMSE against lidar-derived depth. Additional metrics for depth ordering, object-level scale consistency, far-range behavior, uncertainty under radar noise, and adverse weather/night conditions would better support the real-world robustness claims.
